title: Lean Six Sigma Yellow Belt
variant_label: Six Sigma Yellow Belt Real-Spec Practice
content_provenance: Original practice items authored from the Lean Six Sigma Yellow Belt body of knowledge (DMAIC and foundational quality concepts). Not a capture of past questions.
source_label: Lean Six Sigma Yellow Belt practice bank

items.stem: A process improvement team is drafting its project charter and the sponsor asks which element must be documented to authorize the team's work and define its boundaries. Which element belongs in the charter?
options: The business case, problem statement, goal, scope, and team roles
The detailed statistical analysis plan and hypothesis tests
The individual performance ratings of each team member
The final solution design and its return on investment calculation
items.explanation: The project charter in the Define phase establishes the business case, problem and goal statements, scope boundaries, milestones, and team roles, while analysis and solution design occur in later phases.
items.reference: Lean Six Sigma Yellow Belt Body of Knowledge - Define

items.stem: Members of a new improvement team disagree about why the project exists and who has authority to make decisions. Which Define-phase document resolves these questions?
options: The measurement system analysis report
The project charter, which records the purpose, scope, and authority
The control chart used to monitor the process
The Pareto chart of defect categories
items.explanation: The charter is the foundational Define document that names the problem, goal, scope, stakeholders, milestones, and decision authority, aligning the team before any measurement begins.
items.reference: Lean Six Sigma Yellow Belt Body of Knowledge - Define

items.stem: A hotel wants to improve guest satisfaction, so the team interviews guests, reads online reviews, and surveys frequent travelers. Which Six Sigma term describes the input gathered from these sources?
options: Cost of Poor Quality
Statistical Process Control
Voice of the Customer
Critical to Quality
items.explanation: Collecting and analyzing customer needs, expectations, and feedback from multiple channels is the Voice of the Customer activity, which later yields measurable Critical to Quality requirements.
items.reference: Lean Six Sigma Yellow Belt Body of Knowledge - Define

items.stem: After gathering customer feedback, the team must translate a broad need such as a hotel that feels clean into something measurable. What does Six Sigma call this measurable customer requirement?
options: A Voice of the Process metric
A Common Cause of variation
A Standard Operating Procedure
A Critical to Quality characteristic
items.explanation: A Critical to Quality characteristic converts a general customer need into a specific, measurable requirement that the process can be designed and monitored against.
items.reference: Lean Six Sigma Yellow Belt Body of Knowledge - Define

items.stem: Before mapping detailed steps, a team wants a one-page overview showing the process boundaries, the main steps, and who supplies inputs and receives outputs. Which Define tool should the team use?
options: A SIPOC diagram
A control chart
A scatter plot
A Gage R&R study
items.explanation: A SIPOC diagram summarizes Suppliers, Inputs, Process steps, Outputs, and Customers at a high level, making it an effective scoping tool before detailed process mapping.
items.reference: Lean Six Sigma Yellow Belt Body of Knowledge - Define

items.stem: A team writes a problem statement that says the company should buy new software because the order entry process is bad. Why is this statement weak for a Define-phase charter?
options: It is limited to a single department
It prescribes a solution and describes the problem vaguely
It contains too many numerical measurements
It names the process owner and the sponsor
items.explanation: A good problem statement describes the gap between current and desired performance with facts and scope but does not prescribe a solution, and this draft embeds a solution while using the vague word bad.
items.reference: Lean Six Sigma Yellow Belt Body of Knowledge - Define

items.stem: A project charter must include a goal statement. Which goal statement is written in an acceptable Define-phase form?
options: Investigate whether order errors might be a problem
Install a new enterprise system to eliminate errors
Reduce order entry errors from 8 percent to below 2 percent by June 30
Make the order process much better as soon as possible
items.explanation: An effective goal statement is specific, measurable, time-bound, and free of a chosen solution, so the baseline-to-target improvement with a deadline is correct while the others are vague, exploratory, or solution-driven.
items.reference: Lean Six Sigma Yellow Belt Body of Knowledge - Define

items.stem: The charter team is defining scope. Which entry is an example of an item that should be listed under in-scope for an order-to-cash improvement project?
options: The payroll process managed by the finance department
The supplier selection process owned by procurement
The annual marketing campaign planning process
The order entry steps performed by the inside sales team
items.explanation: In-scope items are the processes the team will actually improve, and the order entry steps belong to the order-to-cash process, while payroll, supplier selection, and marketing planning lie outside its boundary.
items.reference: Lean Six Sigma Yellow Belt Body of Knowledge - Define

items.stem: During Define, a team identifies everyone who affects or is affected by the process change and assesses their interest and influence. What is this Define-phase activity called?
options: Stakeholder analysis
Measurement system analysis
Root cause analysis
Capability analysis
items.explanation: Stakeholder analysis identifies the people and groups with an interest in or influence over the project and helps the team plan communication and engagement before changes are implemented.
items.reference: Lean Six Sigma Yellow Belt Body of Knowledge - Define

items.stem: A Yellow Belt is assigned to a project and needs someone to remove organizational barriers and approve resources. Which Define-phase role normally performs this function?
options: The control chart operator
The project sponsor or champion
The data entry clerk
The external auditor
items.explanation: The sponsor or champion provides authority, resources, and barrier removal, while the Yellow Belt supports the project team and daily improvement work under that sponsorship.
items.reference: Lean Six Sigma Yellow Belt Body of Knowledge - Define

items.stem: A customer says they want a quick response to support tickets, and the team uses this statement to develop a measurable requirement of resolving tickets within four hours. Which pairing does this illustrate?
options: A common cause translated into a special cause
A discrete measure translated into a continuous measure
A Voice of the Customer statement translated into a Critical to Quality requirement
A control limit translated into a specification limit
items.explanation: Translating a qualitative customer statement into a specific measurable requirement is exactly the Voice of the Customer to Critical to Quality conversion that makes customer needs actionable for the process.
items.reference: Lean Six Sigma Yellow Belt Body of Knowledge - Define

items.stem: A team has finished drafting its charter, problem statement, goal, scope, and SIPOC. What typically happens next at the end of the Define phase?
options: The team immediately implements a permanent solution to the problem
The team disbands because the project is complete
The team asks the customer to operate the process for a week
The charter is reviewed and approved by the sponsor at a tollgate before measurement begins
items.explanation: Define concludes with a tollgate review where the sponsor approves the charter, confirming alignment and authorizing the team to proceed into the Measure phase.
items.reference: Lean Six Sigma Yellow Belt Body of Knowledge - Define

items.stem: A management team is choosing which improvement project to fund. Which criterion best indicates a strong candidate for a Lean Six Sigma project?
options: It addresses a significant, recurring problem with measurable impact on customers or cost
It is the easiest project with no measurable effect on the business
It affects only one employee and happens once a year
It has already been solved so the team can claim a quick win
items.explanation: Good projects target meaningful, chronic problems whose improvement can be measured and tied to customer or business results, whereas trivial or already-solved efforts waste team capacity.
items.reference: Lean Six Sigma Yellow Belt Body of Knowledge - Define

items.stem: A well-written Define-phase problem statement should answer which key questions about the situation?
options: What the final solution will look like and who will build it
What is wrong, where and when it occurs, how big the gap is, and what the impact is
Which vendor should be selected and at what price
Which team member caused the problem and when
items.explanation: A strong problem statement quantifies the what, where, when, magnitude, and impact of the gap without assigning blame or prescribing a solution, which are common defining mistakes.
items.reference: Lean Six Sigma Yellow Belt Body of Knowledge - Define

items.stem: A team completes the Define phase and wants to ensure the improved process has ongoing accountability after the project ends. Which role should the charter identify for this purpose?
options: The data analyst
The customer
The process owner
The external consultant
items.explanation: The process owner is accountable for the process performance and for sustaining improvements after the project closes, so the charter should name this role from the start.
items.reference: Lean Six Sigma Yellow Belt Body of Knowledge - Define

items.stem: A team wants to see every step of the current order fulfillment process, including decision points and rework loops, to find where delays occur. Which Measure-phase tool is most appropriate?
options: A project charter
A cause-and-effect diagram
A control plan
A detailed process flowchart
items.explanation: A detailed flowchart maps the actual sequence of steps, decisions, and loops so the team can locate delays and non-value-added activity, whereas the other tools serve scope, analysis, or control purposes.
items.reference: Lean Six Sigma Yellow Belt Body of Knowledge - Measure

items.stem: A team is classifying the measurements it will collect. Which of the following is a continuous, or variable, data type?
options: The time in minutes to process a customer order
The number of defects found on an invoice
Whether an order was on time or late
The color category of a product option
items.explanation: Time measured on a continuous scale is variable data, while counts of defects are discrete, pass-or-fail results are attribute data, and color categories are nominal, so the processing time is continuous.
items.reference: Lean Six Sigma Yellow Belt Body of Knowledge - Measure

items.stem: A team records whether each delivered package arrived damaged or undamaged. Which type of data does this produce?
options: Ordinal ranking data
Attribute, or discrete, data
Continuous data
Ratio data with a true zero
items.explanation: Pass-or-fail classification such as defective or not defective produces attribute data, which counts occurrences in categories rather than measuring on a continuous scale.
items.reference: Lean Six Sigma Yellow Belt Body of Knowledge - Measure

items.stem: Two analysts count defects differently because they disagree about what counts as a defect. What should the team create first to ensure consistent measurement?
options: A fishbone diagram of causes
A pilot implementation plan
An operational definition of the defect
A control chart with fixed limits
items.explanation: An operational definition states precisely how a characteristic is measured and what qualifies, removing ambiguity so different people collect comparable data before analysis.
items.reference: Lean Six Sigma Yellow Belt Body of Knowledge - Measure

items.stem: Before collecting data, a team decides what to measure, how to measure it, who will collect it, when, and where. What is this Measure-phase deliverable called?
options: A control plan
A Pareto chart
A solution selection matrix
A data collection plan
items.explanation: A data collection plan specifies the measures, operational definitions, sampling, responsibilities, and timing so the data is reliable and answers the project questions.
items.reference: Lean Six Sigma Yellow Belt Body of Knowledge - Measure

items.stem: A team discovers that two operators get different readings from the same gauge on the same parts. Which Measure-phase study addresses this measurement-system concern?
options: A measurement system analysis, such as a Gage R&R study
A process capability analysis
A Pareto analysis of defect types
A five why analysis of causes
items.explanation: Gage R&R is part of measurement system analysis and quantifies repeatability and reproducibility so the team knows whether observed variation comes from the process or the measurement system.
items.reference: Lean Six Sigma Yellow Belt Body of Knowledge - Measure

items.stem: A scale consistently reads three pounds too high but gives the same reading each time. How is this measurement system best described?
options: It is neither accurate nor precise
It is precise but not accurate
It is accurate but not precise
It is both accurate and precise
items.explanation: Consistency of repeated readings indicates precision, while the constant offset from the true value indicates a lack of accuracy, so the system is precise but biased.
items.reference: Lean Six Sigma Yellow Belt Body of Knowledge - Measure

items.stem: Why must a team evaluate the measurement system before trusting process data in the Measure phase?
options: Measurement systems never change over time
Measurement data is always more accurate than process data
Measurement variation can inflate or hide the true process variation
Measurement studies replace the need to collect process data
items.explanation: If the measurement system itself contributes significant variation or bias, the team may draw wrong conclusions about the process, so measurement system analysis is a prerequisite for valid data.
items.reference: Lean Six Sigma Yellow Belt Body of Knowledge - Measure

items.stem: A process cycle time dataset contains one extreme outlier that raises the arithmetic average well above most values. Which measure of central tendency best represents a typical value in this situation?
options: The mean
The range
The standard deviation
The median
items.explanation: The median is resistant to extreme values, so it describes the typical value better than the mean when outliers are present, while range and standard deviation describe spread rather than center.
items.reference: Lean Six Sigma Yellow Belt Body of Knowledge - Measure

items.stem: Two processes have the same average cycle time, but process A has a much larger standard deviation than process B. What does this indicate about process A?
options: Its individual cycle times vary more widely around the average
Its average cycle time is higher than that of process B
It produces fewer units than process B
Its measurement system is invalid
items.explanation: Standard deviation measures the spread of individual values around the mean, so a larger value means the cycle times are more dispersed even though the averages match.
items.reference: Lean Six Sigma Yellow Belt Body of Knowledge - Measure

items.stem: A team plots the frequency of cycle-time values in ordered intervals to see the shape, center, and spread of the distribution. Which tool is being used?
options: A SIPOC diagram
A histogram
A Pareto chart
A control chart
items.explanation: A histogram shows the distribution of a continuous measure by grouping values into bins, revealing center, spread, and shape such as skew or multiple peaks.
items.reference: Lean Six Sigma Yellow Belt Body of Knowledge - Measure

items.stem: An overall defect rate looks acceptable, but the team suspects one shift performs far worse than the others. What measurement practice will reveal this difference?
options: Removing the worst shift from the dataset
Increasing the sample size for the best shift only
Stratifying the data by shift before analysis
Averaging all shifts into a single number
items.explanation: Stratification separates data into meaningful subgroups such as shifts, so hidden differences are exposed instead of being masked by an overall average.
items.reference: Lean Six Sigma Yellow Belt Body of Knowledge - Measure

items.stem: An operator needs a simple, structured form to tally how often each defect category occurs as it happens on the line. Which data collection tool fits best?
options: A control chart
A Gage R&R study
A force-field analysis
A check sheet
items.explanation: A check sheet is a structured tally form designed for collecting and organizing defect counts at the point of occurrence, making later Pareto analysis straightforward.
items.reference: Lean Six Sigma Yellow Belt Body of Knowledge - Measure

items.stem: Why does the Measure phase establish the current, or baseline, performance of the process?
options: To quantify the starting point so later improvements can be objectively verified
To prove the process cannot be improved
To set the final specification limits
To select the project team members
items.explanation: A baseline gives a factual starting point against which the team measures the effect of changes, so improvement claims are supported by a before-and-after comparison.
items.reference: Lean Six Sigma Yellow Belt Body of Knowledge - Measure

items.stem: A team cannot measure every transaction, so it selects a representative subset to analyze. What is this subset called?
options: A control limit
A sample
A population
A specification
items.explanation: A sample is the subset drawn from the larger population, and when selected representatively its statistics can be used to estimate the behavior of the whole process.
items.reference: Lean Six Sigma Yellow Belt Body of Knowledge - Measure

items.stem: After measuring a high defect rate, a team wants to determine the underlying reason the defects occur rather than just describing the symptoms. What is the goal of this Analyze-phase work?
options: To write the control plan and standard work
To define the project scope and charter
To identify and verify the root cause of the problem
To select the final solution and set a budget
items.explanation: Root cause analysis in the Analyze phase seeks the fundamental reason a problem occurs and verifies it with data, so the team can later address the cause rather than the symptom.
items.reference: Lean Six Sigma Yellow Belt Body of Knowledge - Analyze

items.stem: A team brainstorms potential causes of late deliveries and organizes them into categories such as methods, machines, materials, and people. Which tool are they using?
options: A control chart
A histogram
A process capability index
A cause-and-effect, or fishbone, diagram
items.explanation: The cause-and-effect or Ishikawa diagram arranges potential causes under standard categories to structure brainstorming and guide further verification.
items.reference: Lean Six Sigma Yellow Belt Body of Knowledge - Analyze

items.stem: Starting from a problem, a team repeatedly asks why until it reaches a fundamental cause it can act on. Which Analyze technique is this?
options: The five why technique
The five S method
The SIPOC method
The Gage R&R method
items.explanation: The five why technique drills from a symptom to an actionable root cause by repeatedly asking why, though the number of whys can be more or fewer than five depending on the situation.
items.reference: Lean Six Sigma Yellow Belt Body of Knowledge - Analyze

items.stem: A team notices that a few defect categories account for most of the total defects and wants to prioritize where to focus. Which principle and tool apply here?
options: The Hawthorne effect, shown with a scatter plot
The Pareto principle, shown with a Pareto chart
The central limit theorem, shown with a control chart
The theory of constraints, shown with a histogram
items.explanation: The Pareto principle holds that a small number of causes usually produce most of the effect, and a Pareto chart orders categories by frequency so the vital few are addressed first.
items.reference: Lean Six Sigma Yellow Belt Body of Knowledge - Analyze

items.stem: When constructing a Pareto chart from defect data, how should the category bars be arranged?
options: In random order to avoid bias
By the date each defect was first observed
In descending order of frequency from left to right
Alphabetically by category name
items.explanation: Pareto charts rank categories from most to least frequent so the largest contributors are visually obvious and can be prioritized for action.
items.reference: Lean Six Sigma Yellow Belt Body of Knowledge - Analyze

items.stem: A team suspects that higher oven temperature is associated with more coating defects and plots temperature against defect count for many batches. Which tool are they using?
options: A Pareto chart
A SIPOC diagram
A control plan
A scatter plot
items.explanation: A scatter plot displays paired values of two variables to reveal whether they are related and the direction of the relationship, supporting a hypothesis about cause and effect.
items.reference: Lean Six Sigma Yellow Belt Body of Knowledge - Analyze

items.stem: After brainstorming many possible causes, what should the team do before declaring a root cause confirmed?
options: Verify the suspected cause against data to show it truly drives the problem
Accept the cause that the most senior member suggested
Select the cause that is easiest to fix without checking data
Stop analysis as soon as one cause is listed
items.explanation: Brainstorming produces hypotheses, so the team must test a suspected cause with data or direct observation to confirm it actually influences the problem before investing in solutions.
items.reference: Lean Six Sigma Yellow Belt Body of Knowledge - Analyze

items.stem: A team generates a long list of possible causes and needs to narrow it to the few the group agrees are most likely. Which technique helps the team prioritize the list efficiently?
options: Writing a control plan
Multi-voting on the candidate causes
Calculating the process capability index
Plotting a control chart of defects
items.explanation: Multi-voting lets a group quickly reduce a large list of candidates to the most supported ones for deeper investigation, without lengthy debate over every item.
items.reference: Lean Six Sigma Yellow Belt Body of Knowledge - Analyze

items.stem: How does the five why technique differ from a cause-and-effect diagram during analysis?
options: Five whys is used only in Control, while a cause-and-effect diagram is used only in Define
Five whys proves causation, while a cause-and-effect diagram cannot show causes
Five whys drills a single line of reasoning, while a cause-and-effect diagram broadens to many candidate causes
Five whys requires statistical software, while a cause-and-effect diagram does not
items.explanation: The cause-and-effect diagram expands the search across many potential causes at once, whereas the five why technique follows one causal chain in depth, and both still require data verification.
items.reference: Lean Six Sigma Yellow Belt Body of Knowledge - Analyze

items.stem: A team wants to rank potential failure modes by severity, likelihood of occurrence, and ability to detect them before the failures happen. Which Analyze tool is designed for this?
options: A check sheet
A run chart
A stakeholder analysis
A failure mode and effects analysis
items.explanation: Failure mode and effects analysis scores failure modes on severity, occurrence, and detection to prioritize risks and preventive actions before problems reach the customer.
items.reference: Lean Six Sigma Yellow Belt Body of Knowledge - Analyze

items.stem: A team wants to confirm whether a change in material actually lowered the average defect rate using a formal comparison of before and after data. What category of analytical method does this represent?
options: Hypothesis testing to compare the before and after results
Creating a control plan for the process
Writing the project charter
Building a SIPOC diagram
items.explanation: Hypothesis testing provides a statistical basis for deciding whether an observed difference between groups is real rather than due to chance, supporting evidence-based conclusions in Analyze.
items.reference: Lean Six Sigma Yellow Belt Body of Knowledge - Analyze

items.stem: A team says the problem is that too many invoices are wrong. Why is this less useful than identifying the root cause behind the wrong invoices?
options: It includes the project goal and deadline
It describes the symptom rather than the underlying cause the team can eliminate
It is more measurable than a root cause statement
It identifies the process owner by name
items.explanation: Stating a symptom only tells the team what is observed, not why it happens, so without the root cause any fix risks treating the effect while the cause persists.
items.reference: Lean Six Sigma Yellow Belt Body of Knowledge - Analyze

items.stem: An Improve-phase team has generated several possible solutions to a verified root cause. Which approach is best for selecting the solution to implement?
options: Select the most expensive option to appear serious
Let the newest team member decide alone
Evaluate options against agreed criteria such as impact, effort, cost, and risk
Choose the first idea that was suggested to save time
items.explanation: A structured evaluation against criteria such as impact, effort, cost, and risk selects the solution most likely to address the verified cause within constraints rather than relying on speed, cost, or authority.
items.reference: Lean Six Sigma Yellow Belt Body of Knowledge - Improve

items.stem: A team runs a small test of a proposed change, studies the results against its prediction, and then standardizes or adjusts the change. Which improvement cycle does this describe?
options: Define-Measure-Analyze-Design
First-In-First-Out
Sort-Set-Shine-Standardize-Sustain
Plan-Do-Check-Act
items.explanation: Plan-Do-Check-Act is an iterative cycle in which a change is planned, tested on a small scale, evaluated against expectations, and then standardized or revised.
items.reference: Lean Six Sigma Yellow Belt Body of Knowledge - Improve

items.stem: In Lean thinking, which of the following is classified as one of the classic forms of waste?
options: Waiting for materials or information between steps
Producing exactly to customer demand
Training employees to do their jobs well
Maintaining equipment in good working order
items.explanation: Waiting is one of the classic Lean wastes, while producing to demand, training people, and maintaining equipment are value-adding or necessary activities rather than waste.
items.reference: Lean Six Sigma Yellow Belt Body of Knowledge - Improve

items.stem: Workers regularly walk across the plant to fetch tools kept far from their workstations. Which Lean waste does this example illustrate?
options: Defects
Motion
Overproduction
Inventory
items.explanation: Unnecessary movement of people, such as walking to retrieve distant tools, is the waste of motion, while the other options describe different wastes such as making too much, excess stock, or faulty output.
items.reference: Lean Six Sigma Yellow Belt Body of Knowledge - Improve

items.stem: A workplace improvement effort focuses on sorting, setting in order, shining, standardizing, and sustaining. Which Lean method does this describe?
options: The SIPOC scoping method
The Gage R&R measurement method
The 5S workplace organization method
The five why root cause method
items.explanation: 5S is a workplace organization method whose five steps, commonly translated as sort, set in order, shine, standardize, and sustain, create and maintain an efficient, safe work area.
items.reference: Lean Six Sigma Yellow Belt Body of Knowledge - Improve

items.stem: A facility holds a focused, short-duration event in which a cross-functional team redesigns a work area and implements improvements on the spot. What is this Lean activity called?
options: A capability study
A tollgate review
A control chart review
A kaizen event
items.explanation: A kaizen event is a concentrated improvement workshop where a team analyzes a process and implements changes rapidly, often over a few days, to achieve quick and visible gains.
items.reference: Lean Six Sigma Yellow Belt Body of Knowledge - Improve

items.stem: A production line is redesigned so a part can only be inserted in the correct orientation, preventing an assembly error. Which Lean concept does this illustrate?
options: Mistake-proofing, or poka-yoke
Total productive maintenance
Value stream mapping
Standard deviation
items.explanation: Mistake-proofing, or poka-yoke, designs the process or tooling so errors are prevented or immediately detected, making it hard or impossible to perform a step incorrectly.
items.reference: Lean Six Sigma Yellow Belt Body of Knowledge - Improve

items.stem: Before rolling a solution out across all locations, an Improve-phase team tests it at one site for a short period. What is a key reason to pilot the change?
options: To skip verifying the root cause
To learn and refine the solution on a small scale before full deployment
To guarantee the solution cannot fail anywhere
To avoid measuring whether the change worked
items.explanation: A pilot limits the cost and risk of a change while providing real-world evidence to refine the solution, increasing the likelihood of success when it is deployed more widely.
items.reference: Lean Six Sigma Yellow Belt Body of Knowledge - Improve

items.stem: A team reviews its process map and finds several approval steps that customers do not value and that add delay without changing the output. What should the team focus on in the Improve phase?
options: Keeping all steps but working faster on each
Automating every step without questioning its value
Eliminating or simplifying the non-value-added steps
Adding more approvals to increase control
items.explanation: Lean improvement targets non-value-added activity for elimination or simplification first, and automating or speeding up a step that has no customer value does not remove the underlying waste.
items.reference: Lean Six Sigma Yellow Belt Body of Knowledge - Improve

items.stem: An Improve team must ensure its chosen changes are actually put into practice and that people know what to do differently. Which action should accompany the solution implementation?
options: Announce the change only after a year has passed
Leave each operator to keep using the old method
Remove all documentation to encourage flexibility
Communicate the changes and train the people who perform the process
items.explanation: Successful implementation requires communicating the change and training the workforce so the new method is adopted consistently, otherwise the process reverts to the old behavior.
items.reference: Lean Six Sigma Yellow Belt Body of Knowledge - Improve

items.stem: After an improvement is deployed, the team documents what will be monitored, by whom, how often, and what action to take if the process drifts. What is this Control-phase document called?
options: A control plan
A project charter
A cause-and-effect diagram
A Voice of the Customer study
items.explanation: A control plan specifies the monitored characteristics, measurement methods, sampling frequency, responsibility, and reaction plan needed to hold the gains after the project ends.
items.reference: Lean Six Sigma Yellow Belt Body of Knowledge - Control

items.stem: A team wants to monitor a process over time and distinguish normal variation from unusual changes that require action. Which Control-phase tool is designed for this?
options: A force-field analysis
A statistical process control chart
A Pareto chart of defect categories
A SIPOC diagram
items.explanation: A control chart plots process data over time with statistically derived limits so the team can separate routine common-cause variation from special-cause signals that call for investigation.
items.reference: Lean Six Sigma Yellow Belt Body of Knowledge - Control

items.stem: A process is stable and all output remains inside the control limits with no unusual patterns. What type of variation is present?
options: No variation of any kind
Variation caused only by the customer
Common-cause variation that is inherent in the process
Special-cause variation from an assignable source
items.explanation: When a process is stable and points stay within limits without patterns, only common-cause variation is present, and reacting to it as if it were special would be over-adjustment.
items.reference: Lean Six Sigma Yellow Belt Body of Knowledge - Control

items.stem: On a control chart, several consecutive points fall well outside the upper control limit. What should the process operator do?
options: Ignore the points because production must continue
Immediately recalculate the control limits to include the points
Assume the chart is broken and stop recording data
Investigate for a special cause and take corrective action using the reaction plan
items.explanation: Points outside the control limits are a classic out-of-control signal indicating a special cause, so the operator should follow the reaction plan and investigate rather than ignore or alter the limits.
items.reference: Lean Six Sigma Yellow Belt Body of Knowledge - Control

items.stem: A team wants to lock in an improved method so every operator performs the task the same proven way. Which Control-phase action supports this goal?
options: Documenting and implementing standard work for the task
Returning to the previous informal method
Allowing each operator to choose any method
Postponing documentation until the next project
items.explanation: Standard work documents the best known method and its key steps so the process stays consistent and the gains are not lost once the improvement team disbands.
items.reference: Lean Six Sigma Yellow Belt Body of Knowledge - Control

items.stem: A control plan specifies that if a monitored measurement exceeds its limit, the operator must notify the line lead and stop the batch. What part of the control plan is this?
options: The measurement system analysis
The reaction or response plan
The problem statement
The data collection frequency
items.explanation: The reaction plan states the specific action to take when a monitored characteristic goes out of control, ensuring a consistent and timely response rather than an ad hoc one.
items.reference: Lean Six Sigma Yellow Belt Body of Knowledge - Control

items.stem: A work area uses labeled floor markings, shadow boards, and visible status displays so anyone can see whether the process is operating normally. Which Control-phase practice is this?
options: Root cause analysis
Hypothesis testing
Visual management
Value stream mapping
items.explanation: Visual management makes process status and standards visible at a glance so deviations are noticed and corrected quickly, helping sustain control.
items.reference: Lean Six Sigma Yellow Belt Body of Knowledge - Control

items.stem: At the end of a successful Lean Six Sigma project, the team transfers responsibility for monitoring the improved process to the process owner. Which Control-phase deliverable documents this handover?
options: The original project charter with no measurements
The brainstormed list of all possible causes
The team meeting minutes from the Define phase
The completed control plan and updated standard work
items.explanation: Project closeout in Control hands the process owner the control plan, standard work, and monitoring responsibilities so the improvements are maintained after the team disbands.
items.reference: Lean Six Sigma Yellow Belt Body of Knowledge - Control
